Guide 01 · Saving & compounding4 min read

How do you get to your first $100,000?

Charlie Munger said the first $100,000 is the hardest. He was right — and the math shows exactly why, and why it gets easier from there.

Why the first $100,000 is the hardest

Early on, your contributions do almost all the work. Your investments haven't had time to compound yet, so the balance grows mostly because you keep adding money.

Say you invest $500 a month and earn an 8% average annual return. It takes about 10.6 years to reach $100,000 — and of that $100,000, you contributed about $63,750 yourself. Investment growth added only about $36,250.

You did most of the work. That's why it feels slow.

First $100k: 10.6 years. Second $100k: 5.7 years.

Same $500 a month, same 8% return. The second hundred thousand arrives nearly twice as fast — with no extra effort from you.

Then it flips

Keep doing the exact same thing and compounding takes over. At 8%, your money roughly doubles every 9 years — divide 72 by 8; that's the rule of 72. Once the balance is big enough, the growth on the balance starts doing more than your monthly contributions do.

Same habit, very different speed

$500/month at an illustrative 8% average annual return

First $100k
10.6 yrs
Second $100k
5.7 yrs

The first $100,000 is a savings game. Everything after it is a patience game.

How to actually get there

  1. Automate it on paydayPick an amount and have it move the day your pay lands. If you have to decide every month, some months you won't.
  2. Start with what you can, then raise it$500 a month gets there in about 10.6 years at 8%; $1,000 a month takes about 6.4 years. But $100 a month beats $0 a month — the habit matters more than the starting amount.
  3. Put it somewhere it can growIn Canada, a TFSA holding a broad market ETF is the usual starting point: the growth is tax-free, and one fund holds hundreds of companies, so you're not betting on a single stock.
  4. Don't stop when the market dropsA downturn means the same $500 buys more. The people who reach $100,000 aren't the ones who timed it perfectly — they're the ones who kept going when it felt pointless.

What slows people down

  • Waiting to start. Every year you wait, the monthly amount needed goes up. Starting beats waiting — that's the whole story of compounding.
  • Trying to pick winners. Beating the market consistently is rare — about 90% of professional fund managers underperform the S&P 500 over 15 years. Your job isn't to outsmart them. It's to stay invested.
  • Stopping and starting. Pausing contributions for a year doesn't just cost that year's deposits — it costs decades of growth on those deposits.
“The first $100,000 is a b*tch, but you gotta do it.”— Charlie Munger, on why the first milestone is the hard one

The bottom line

The first $100,000 feels like pushing a boulder uphill because, mostly, it is. Your money isn't doing much yet — you are. But once you're past it, the hill starts sloping the other way. Start with whatever you can, automate it, and let time do the rest.

All numbers assume an 8% average annual return and are illustrative only — actual returns vary year to year and are never guaranteed. Educational only, not financial advice.

Guide 02 · Getting started3 min read

How to invest your first $1,000

Your first $1,000 is the hardest money to invest — not because the amount is big, but because it's the first time. Here's the whole process in four steps.

The four steps

  1. Kill high-interest debt firstIf you have credit card debt at ~20% interest, paying it off beats any investment — no investment reliably returns 20% a year, so clearing it is a guaranteed 20% “return.” If your only debt is a student loan at a low rate, that's different: you can invest and pay it down at the same time. High-interest debt is the emergency; everything else can wait.
  2. Open a TFSAIn Canada, the Tax-Free Savings Account is where your first $1,000 should usually go. Money inside a TFSA grows tax-free — you never pay tax on the growth, and never pay tax when you take it out. Check your contribution room in CRA My Account before you deposit; it builds up every year you've been a resident over 18, so most people in their twenties have more room than they think.
  3. Buy a broad market ETFWith $1,000, don't try to pick one winning stock. Buy a broad market ETF — a single fund that holds hundreds of companies at once. If one company struggles, the other hundreds carry the weight. You don't need to research 500 companies; you need one decision: a diversified fund, bought once, left alone.
  4. Automate what comes nextThe $1,000 is the start, not the plan. Set up an automatic contribution — $50, $100, whatever fits — every payday. This is where the real growth happens.

Why the habit beats the amount

Here's what the math says about a first $1,000 at an 8% average annual return:

One deposit vs. one deposit + a habit

At an illustrative 8% average annual return

The first $1,000 opens the account. The habit builds the wealth.

Of that ~$160,000, you'd only have put in about $37,000. The rest is growth — but only because the monthly deposit kept showing up.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Waiting for the perfect moment. There isn't one. The market moves up and down every year, and people who wait for a dip usually wait for years.
  • Picking a single stock. One company can fall 50% and never come back. A broad market fund spreads that risk across hundreds of companies.
  • Checking it every day. Daily moves are noise. The $1,000 you invest today matters in 10 years, not on Thursday.

The bottom line

Kill the expensive debt, open a TFSA, buy one diversified fund, and automate the next deposit. That's it. The amount matters less than starting — $1,000 invested beats $0 invested every time.

Guide 03 · Debt payoff5 min read

How do you pay off student loans fast?

Student loans feel endless because the balance barely seems to move. It does move — just slowly, if you're only paying the minimum. Here's how to make it move faster.

Step 1: Know what you actually owe

In Canada, your student loan is usually two loans stapled together — and they don't cost the same:

0%

The federal portion

The government permanently eliminated interest on Canada Student Loans in April 2023. This part costs you nothing to carry — it never grows while you leave it alone.

~5.7%

The provincial portion

This one may charge interest, depending on your province. Ontario charges prime + 1% (about 5.7% in late 2026). Some provinces — like B.C. and Manitoba — charge 0%.

Check your NSLSC statement and find your split. If your provincial portion is the only part charging interest, that's the part to attack first.

Step 2: Attack the highest rate first

This is called the avalanche method: put every extra dollar toward the highest-interest debt, while paying the minimum on the rest.

It works because interest is the only thing making a loan grow. A dollar against a 5.7% loan saves you more than a dollar against a 0% loan — the 0% loan doesn't grow at all while you focus elsewhere.

Step 3: Raise the payment — the math is dramatic

Take a $30,000 loan at 5.7% as an example:

Monthly paymentTime to pay offTotal interest paid
~$329 (minimum)10 years~$9,427
$4007.7 years~$7,178
$5005.9 years~$5,397

+$171/month ≈ $4,000 saved and 4 years back.

Going from the minimum to $500 a month changes the whole picture. You don't need a huge raise to make a huge difference.

Steps 4–6: The details that matter

  1. Make extra payments hit the principalWhen you pay extra, tell your lender you want it applied to the principal — the actual balance — not just used to push your next due date forward. Some servicers treat extra payments as advance payments by default, which doesn't shrink the loan as fast. After any extra payment, check your statement and confirm the balance dropped by the full amount.
  2. Use windfalls — and claim the tax creditTax refunds, work bonuses, birthday money: send lump sums straight to the highest-rate portion. A $1,000 lump sum against a 5.7% loan saves far more than $1,000 over the life of the loan, because it also kills all the interest that $1,000 would have generated. And don't forget the student loan interest tax credit — interest paid on government student loans earns a federal and provincial non-refundable tax credit. Keep your NSLSC interest statement and claim it.
  3. Don't drain your emergency fund to go fasterPaying a loan off fast is good. Paying it off so fast that a flat tire lands on a credit card at ~20% is not. Keep a small buffer — even $500 to $1,000 — then attack the loan. And if payments are genuinely unmanageable, don't just stop paying: the Repayment Assistance Plan can lower or pause payments without damaging your credit the way a missed payment would.

The bottom line

The fastest way to kill a student loan is a bigger monthly payment aimed at the highest-rate portion. Know your split, pay extra against the part that charges interest, and let the 0% federal portion wait its turn.

Example numbers assume a $30,000 balance at 5.7% and are illustrative only. Rates change — check your NSLSC statement for your actual rates. Educational only, not financial advice.
